title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: What most clearly separates a workflow from an agent?

options.text: Whether the system calls a language model at all
Whether the code or the model picks each next step
Whether the system can call tools like a calendar
Whether the system takes more than one step to finish

items.stem: A makerspace feature runs three steps in this order for every request: (1) the model pulls the machine name and date out of the student's message, (2) the program looks up that machine on the calendar, (3) the model writes a reply from the result. Who owns the control flow, and why?

options.text: The model, because it writes the final reply
The model, because it reads the student's message
The program, because the order is set in advance
Neither, because the system calls a model twice

items.stem: Which makerspace task is the strongest candidate for a fixed workflow rather than an agent?

options.text: Booking a slot: check availability, reserve it, send a confirmation
Working out why a student's 3D prints keep failing midway
Answering a question that may span several machine manuals
Comparing two machines for a student's unusual project idea

items.stem: In one sentence, explain why a fixed workflow usually costs less per request than an agent for the same booking task.

The team's booking workflow works well, but one request type, such as "book the laser cutter any evening next week when the training room is also free", needs a different number of calendar checks each time. What is the best response?

options.text: Rebuild the whole assistant as one agent for every request
Add a fixed step for every possible number of calendar checks
Drop the calendar check and let the model guess free times
Give only that request type to a step-limited agent loop

items.stem: A teammate says: "An agent is the more advanced design, so our assistant should be an agent everywhere." Give one reason this is a poor rule for choosing.
